  - Also includes cases where there’s significant extension through tissue planes making complete resection unlikely.

Each letter represents different characteristics about how far the cancer may have grown or spread since its initial development.

Pancreatic cancer refers to an abnormal growth of cells within the pancreas that can form tumors and spread to other parts of the body. It typically originates in the ducts or glands of this organ and may lead to various symptoms including abdominal pain, weight loss, jaundice, and digestive issues depending upon its location and progression.

Pancreatic cancer is staged using the TNM system (Tumor, Node, Metastasis) by the American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC), which describes:

- T for tumor size and extent within or outside the pancreas 
- N for lymph node involvement
- M for metastases to distant organs

It's also commonly described in simpler clinical staging from 0 to IV:
Stage 0 - Carcinoma In Situ (abnormal cells only in the lining)
Stage I - Confined to the pancreas with no spread
    IA - Small tumors (<2 cm)
    IB - Larger localized tumors (>2cm but still confined)
II - Locally advanced disease extending beyond head of pancreas into nearby tissues/organs without major nodes involved
III - Spread to regional lymph nodes near the main artery supplying blood to liver
IV - Distant metastasis to other parts of body like lungs/liver/bone/stomach

Diagnosing pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors involves several steps:

1. **Medical History & Symptoms**: Assessing symptoms related to hormone overproduction or abdominal pain.

2. **Blood Tests**:
   - Biochemical markers like Chromogranin A for general screening of NETs.
   - Specific tests depending on suspected hormones produced by tumor such as insulin levels in cases of Insulinoma.

3. **Imaging Studies**:
   - CT scan with contrast 
   - MRI
   - Endoscopic Ultrasound (EUS)
   - PET scans using specific tracers like Octreoscan

4. **Endoscopy Procedures**
   - EUS can provide detailed images near pancreas and allow biopsy if needed
   
5. **Biopsy**: Confirmatory tissue sample analysis through fine needle aspiration during endoscopic ultrasound guided procedure.

6. **Genetic Testing**: In some instances where there's suspicion of hereditary syndromes associated with these tumours.

Each case may require different combinations of above methods tailored according to clinical presentation and availability of resources at healthcare facility. Consultation with an oncologist is recommended for accurate diagnosis and management plan.

Renal cell cancer, also known as renal cell carcinoma or RCC, is a type of kidney cancer that originates in the proximal convoluted tubules of the small tubes in the nephrons within the kidneys. It's one of the most common types of kidney cancers found in adults.

The common symptoms of transitional cell cancer of the renal pelvis and ureter include blood in urine (hematuria), pain or discomfort in the flank area (side part of the back where kidneys lie), frequent urination, painful urination, and abdominal mass. In some cases, patients may also experience fatigue, weight loss, fever, or swelling in legs due to obstruction or blockage by tumor growth.

Research into transitional cell cancer of the renal pelixs and ureter includes various ongoing studies focusing on new treatments, biomarkers, and therapeutic strategies. ClinicalTrials.gov lists several active investigations involving immunotherapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy combinations, and novel agents such as FGFR inhibitors in patients with advanced or metastatic disease where standard therapies have failed.

For precise details including eligibility criteria, contact your healthcare provider or visit https://clinicaltrials.gov/. Always consult a professional before participating in any trial to ensure it's suitable for you given current health status and other factors.

The outlook (prognosis) for children with Wilms tumor and other childhood kidney tumors generally depends on several factors including age at diagnosis, size of the tumor, whether it has spread to nearby lymph nodes or distant organs like lungs or bones, as well as specific genetic features.

For Wilms tumor specifically:
- Overall survival rates exceed 90% in many cases when detected early and treated appropriately.
- The five-year overall survival rate ranges from about 85%-92%, depending largely upon stage at detection; localized disease typically offers better outcomes than advanced stages where cancer may have metastasized beyond the kidneys.

Other less common pediatric renal malignancies such as clear cell sarcoma of the kidney and malignant rhabdoid tumor tend to carry poorer prognoses due to their aggressive nature even if diagnosed earlier compared to Wilms' tumor. Treatment approaches often involve surgery combined with chemotherapy and sometimes radiation therapy tailored according to individual patient characteristics and clinical presentation.

Individuals at higher risk for breast cancer include women over 50 years old, those with a family history of breast or ovarian cancer, individuals carrying BRCA1 or BRCA2 gene mutations, those who started menstruating before age 12 or went through menopause after age 55, never had children or first pregnancy after age 30, have dense breasts, personal history of benign lumps in the breast, previous chest radiation therapy, long-term use of hormone replacement therapies containing estrogen and progesterone, obesity (especially post-menopausal), physical inactivity, alcohol consumption, and certain genetic syndromes like Li-Fraumeni syndrome. Men can also develop breast cancer but it's less common.

The outlook for breast cancer varies depending on several factors including the stage at diagnosis, type of tumor, age, overall health status, and response to treatment. Early-stage breast cancers have very high survival rates; according to the American Cancer Society, about 99% of women with localized (stage I) invasive breast cancer survive five years or more after their initial diagnosis. For later stages, such as regional spread (stages II-III), this rate drops but still remains relatively good around 85%-90%. The prognosis becomes less favorable in cases where there's distant metastasis (Stage IV). Regular screenings can help detect breast cancer early when it’s most treatable. Treatment options include surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, hormone therapy, targeted drug treatments, and immunotherapy. Advances in these areas continue to improve outcomes even for advanced disease states.

Men with certain conditions that increase estrogen levels or reduce testosterone levels are at higher risk of male breast cancer, including those who have had mumps as children, Klinefelter syndrome, cirrhosis, obesity, or exposure to radiation. Men with a family history of BRCA gene mutations (commonly associated with hereditary breast cancer in women) also face an increased risk. Elderly men and those with a personal history of breast disease are additionally more susceptible.

Male breast cancer is staged similarly to female breast cancer using the TNM system (Tumor size, Lymph Node involvement, Metastasis) combined with numerical staging from Stage 0 to IV:

- **Stage 0**: Carcinoma in situ where abnormal cells have not spread beyond ducts or lobules.

- **Stage I**: Tumor smaller than 2 cm that has not spread outside the breast tissue.

- **Stage II**:
    - IA: A tumor no larger than 2cm without lymph node involvement.
    - IB: Presence of small clusters of cancerous cells within axillary nodes measuring less than .5mm, possibly associated with a very tiny (<1 mm) primary tumor in the breast itself.
    - IIA: No tumor detected but there's evidence it may be present; OR a tumor between 2-5 cm with no nodal metastases.
    - IIB: The tumor measures more than 2 cm up to 5 cm and/or involves one to three nearby lymph nodes underarm.

- **Stage III**:
   - IIIA: Larger tumors (>5cm), involving several regional lymph nodes.
   - IIIB: Any sized tumor extending into chest wall or skin causing ulceration/irritation.
   - IIIC: Regardless of tumor size, extensive local/regional lymphatic invasion including internal mammary nodes.

- **Stage IV**: Distant organ/systemic metastasis such as lungs, liver, bones, brain

The outlook (prognosis) for skin cancer varies depending on several factors including type of cancer, stage at diagnosis, location, size, depth of invasion, presence or absence of metastasis, age, overall health status, and response to treatment.

- **Basal Cell Carcinoma**: Generally has an excellent prognosis with early detection and appropriate management; it rarely spreads beyond the original site but can cause local damage if left untreated.
  
- **Squamous Cell Carcinoma**: Also often curable when detected early, though carries higher risk compared to basal cell carcinoma due to potential spread to lymph nodes in advanced stages.

- **Melanoma**: Prognosis ranges from very good to poor, largely dependent upon thickness/stage at time of discovery - thinner tumors have better outcomes while thicker ones that penetrate deeper into tissues carry greater risks including spreading throughout body systems leading potentially fatal consequences without timely intervention.

Regular screening, prompt evaluation of suspicious lesions by dermatologists, adherence to recommended treatments significantly improve survival rates across all types.

People with fair skin, light hair or eye color, those who have had sunburns in the past, individuals with many moles (especially unusual-looking ones), people over 50 years old, those with a family history of melanoma, and anyone frequently exposed to sunlight or UV radiation are at higher risk for developing melanoma. Additionally, having previously had non-melanoma skin cancers also increases one's risk.

Treatments for melanoma include surgery (excision), radiation therapy, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy, and in some cases clinical trials or observational studies. The choice of treatment depends on factors such as tumor thickness, location, stage at diagnosis, and patient health status. Early-stage melanomas often require surgical excision alone, while advanced stages may need combined therapies including immune checkpoint inhibitors, BRAF/MEK inhibitor combinations, or other systemic treatments. Radiation can be used post-surgery to target residual cancer cells or palliatively manage symptoms from metastatic disease. Clinical trial options might involve new drugs or techniques aimed at improving outcomes. Consultation with an oncologist is essential for personalized care planning.

Merkel cell carcinoma is diagnosed through several steps:

1. **Clinical Examination**: A dermatologist or healthcare provider examines any suspicious skin lesion for signs of malignancy.

2. **Biopsy**:
   - **Excisional Biopsy**: The entire lump along with some surrounding tissue may be removed surgically.
   - **Incisional Biopsy**: Only part of the growth might be taken if excising it completely would cause significant cosmetic damage.

3. **Histopathology**: Examining the biopsy under a microscope by a pathologist can confirm whether cancer cells are present and identify them as Merkel cell carcinomas specifically due to their characteristic appearance.

4. **Immunohistochemistry (IHC)**: Special stains help distinguish Merkel cell carcinoma from other types of tumors; these cancers typically show positive staining for cytokeratin 20 but negative for thyroid transcription factor-1 (TTF-1).

5. **Virology Testing**: Given that about 8 out of 10 cases involve infection with Merkel cell polyomavirus (MCV), testing for MCV DNA in tumor samples using PCR techniques aids diagnosis.

6. **Staging Tests**: If confirmed, imaging studies like CT scans, PET/CTs, MRIs etc., assess extent/local spread/metastasis aiding staging which guides treatment planning. 

Each case requires individualized assessment considering clinical presentation & histological features alongside molecular diagnostics when necessary.

To prevent skin cancer, follow these key steps:

1. Use sunscreen with at least SPF 30 that blocks both UVA and UVB rays daily.
2. Wear protective clothing such as long sleeves, pants, hats, and sunglasses when outdoors.
3. Seek shade or avoid sun exposure during peak hours (usually between 10 AM - 4 PM).
4. Avoid tanning beds and excessive sunbathing.
5. Regularly examine your skin for any changes in moles or new growths.

These measures help reduce risk by minimizing harmful ultraviolet radiation exposure from sunlight and artificial sources.

Plasma cell neoplasm staging is primarily done for multiple myeloma using several systems, with the most common being the Revised International Staging System (R-ISS):

1. **Stage I**: Patients have one or no risk factors (beta-2 microglobulin <5.5 g/L and albumin >35g/L).
2. **Stage II**: Does not fit into Stage I or III criteria; patients may have normal levels of beta-2-microglobulin but low albumin, or vice versa.
3. **Stage III**: Patients meet at least one high-risk factor (beta-2 microglobulin ≥ 5.5 g/L).

Additionally, there's an sR-ISS system that incorporates genetic markers to refine prognosis:

- **sR-ISS Low Risk** (<4 years median survival)
- **sR-ISS Intermediate-Risk 1** (approximately 6-year median survival)
- **sR-ISS Intermediate-Risk 2** (~4-year median survival)
- **sR-ISS High Risk** (<2 years median survival)

These classifications help in predicting patient outcomes and guiding treatment decisions.

Symptoms of neuroblastoma can vary depending on its location and whether it has spread to other parts of the body but may include:

- Abdominal swelling or pain due to tumor growth in abdomen
- Bone pain or bone tenderness from metastasis (commonly occurs in bones)
- Lumps under skin 
- Fatigue and weakness
- Fever and night sweats
- Difficulty breathing if tumors involve chest cavity
- Eye protrusion if near orbit behind eye

Other less common systemic signs like weight loss, anemia, hypertension etc might also be present. Early stages often show no obvious symptoms until cancer spreads significantly.

Research and clinical trials for neuroblastoma focus on improving treatment outcomes through various approaches including immunotherapy, targeted therapy, chemotherapy modifications, radiation techniques, stem cell transplantation, and combination therapies. Specific ongoing studies may involve monoclonal antibodies like chimeric antigen receptor T cells (CAR-T), drugs targeting specific genetic mutations or proteins in cancer cells, vaccine-based treatments, and precision medicine strategies tailored to individual patient characteristics. For the most current information, consulting databases such as ClinicalTrials.gov provides detailed listings of active trials globally.

Non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) is typically diagnosed through several steps:

1. **Medical History & Physical Exam**: A thorough evaluation of symptoms, risk factors, and physical examination.

2. **Imaging Tests**:
   - Chest X-ray 
   - CT scan of the chest

3. **Biopsy**: To confirm diagnosis, tissue or fluid samples can be obtained via various methods such as bronchoscopy, needle biopsy, thoracoscentesis, mediastinoscopy, or video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS).

4. **Pathological Examination**: Biopsied material analyzed under microscope for presence of malignant cells.

5. **Staging**: Once confirmed, additional tests like PET-CT scans, bone scans, MRI may determine if cancer has spread beyond lungs.

Each case might require different approaches depending upon clinical presentation and resources available at healthcare facility. Consultation with pulmonologist or oncologist recommended for accurate assessment and management plan.

Small cell lung cancer (SCLC) is a type of malignant tumor that originates in the epithelial cells lining the bronchi or other air passages within the lungs. It is characterized by small, round癌细胞，翻译成中文：

小细胞肺癌（SCLC）是一种起源于肺部支气管或其他呼吸道上皮细胞的恶性肿瘤。其特点是含有小型、圆形的癌细胞。

注意：在医学术语中，“癌”通常用来指代“cancer”，因此最后部分可以更自然地表达为：“其特点是由较小且形态较为一致的小圆型癌细胞组成。”这样会更加符合中文的习惯表述方式。所以最终答案建议调整如下：

小细胞肺癌（SCLC）是发生于肺部支气管或其它呼吸通道内衬上的上皮细胞的一种恶性肿瘤。这种癌症的特点是由较小且形态较为一致的小圆型癌细胞构成。

The primary treatments for small cell lung cancer (SCLC) include chemotherapy, which is often combined with radiation therapy for both limited-stage and extensive-stage disease. Surgery is rarely an option due to the aggressive nature of SCLC at diagnosis. For some patients, immunotherapy may be used in combination with or as an alternative to standard chemotherapeutic regimens. Targeted therapies might also be considered depending on specific genetic characteristics of the tumor. Palliative care can help manage symptoms and improve quality of life throughout treatment.

Parathyroid cancer is a rare type of tumor that develops in one or more of the parathyroid glands, which are four small endocrine glands located behind the thyroid gland in the neck. This form of cancer typically results in excessive production of parathyroid hormone (PTH), leading to hyperparathyroidism characterized by elevated calcium levels in the blood. Symptoms can include bone pain, kidney stones, frequent urination, nausea, vomiting, fatigue, weakness, and depression among others. Treatment usually involves surgical removal of the affected gland(s).

Parathyroid cancer does not have distinct clinical "stages" like other cancers such as breast or lung cancer (which use staging systems to describe how far the disease has spread). Instead, parathyroid tumors are generally described by their size, whether they are benign adenomas or malignant carcinomas, if there is local invasion into surrounding tissues, regional lymph node involvement, distant metastasis, and hyperparathyroidism status.

However, for grading severity:
- Localized tumor confined to the gland without invading nearby structures indicates an early form.
- Tumors that invade adjacent tissue or cause bone lesions indicate more advanced cases.
- Metastatic parathyroid carcinoma spreads beyond the neck region, often affecting lungs, bones, liver, etc., representing the most severe stage. 

Diagnosis typically involves imaging studies and biochemical tests measuring calcium levels and PTH production. Treatment usually includes surgical removal of the affected gland(s) with possible additional therapies depending on extent and symptoms.

Symptoms of penile cancer can include:

- A growth or sore on the penis
- Bleeding from the tip of the penis not associated with urination 
- Discharge under the foreskin
- Lump on the penis
- Change in color (redness) of the skin on the penis

These symptoms may indicate other conditions as well but warrant prompt evaluation by a healthcare provider if present. Early detection is important for effective treatment.

Research into penile cancer includes various areas such as new treatment methods, improving surgical techniques, developing targeted therapies, and exploring immunotherapy options. ClinicalTrials.gov lists several ongoing studies focusing on different aspects of penile cancer management:

1. **Surgical Techniques**: Improving reconstructive surgery after tumor removal to enhance patient outcomes.

2. **Immunotherapies**: Investigating drugs that boost immune response against tumors.

3. **Targeted Therapies**: Studying medications targeting specific genetic mutations or proteins in penile cancers.

4. **Combination Treatments**: Testing combinations of chemotherapy with radiation therapy or other treatments to improve efficacy while reducing side effects.

5. **Supportive Care Studies**: Researching ways to better manage symptoms like pain and sexual dysfunction associated with this condition.

For detailed information about current clinical trials, visiting ClinicalTrials.gov can provide up-to-date listings relevant to penile cancer patients seeking participation opportunities.

The outlook (prognosis) for pituitary tumors generally depends on their type, size, hormone production effects, and treatment response. Most pituitary adenomas are benign with an excellent prognosis if treated appropriately. Microadenomas (<10mm) often have high cure rates after surgery or radiation therapy. Hormone-secreting tumors can be managed effectively through medications in addition to surgical removal when necessary. In general, patients diagnosed early and receiving proper management typically maintain good quality of life outcomes. However, non-functioning macroadenomas (>10mm) may require more aggressive treatments and could potentially lead to complications such as vision loss if left untreated. Regular follow-up care is essential post-treatment due to possible recurrence risk.

Symptoms of prostate cancer can include:
- Difficulty starting urination or weak urine flow
- Frequent urges to urinate, especially at night
- Painful or burning sensation during urination 
- Blood in urine or semen
- Erectile dysfunction
- Pelvic area discomfort
- Bone pain (if cancer has spread)
However, many men with early stage prostate cancer do not experience noticeable symptoms. Regular screening is important for detection.

Research and clinical trials for prostate cancer focus on various aspects including new treatments, early detection methods, and improving quality of life for patients. Some key areas include:

1. **Immunotherapy**: Trials involving immune checkpoint inhibitors to enhance the body's ability to fight cancer cells.

2. **Targeted Therapies**: Research into drugs that target specific molecules involved in tumor growth or survival.

3. **Hormonal Therapy Enhancements**: Studies aimed at developing more effective hormonal therapies with fewer side effects.

4. **Radiation Techniques**: Improvements in radiation therapy techniques such as proton beam therapy and targeted radiotherapy.

5. **Early Detection Methods**: Development of better biomarkers and imaging technologies for earlier diagnosis.

6. **Combination Treatments**: Clinical studies combining different types of treatment modalities like chemotherapy plus immunotherapy.

7. **Precision Medicine Approaches**: Personalized medicine strategies tailored to individual patient genetics and tumor characteristics.

These ongoing efforts aim to improve outcomes and reduce mortality rates associated with prostate cancer. For detailed information about current trials, one can visit websites like ClinicalTrials.gov.

The common symptoms of colon cancer include persistent changes in bowel habits (such as constipation or diarrhea), blood in stool, abdominal pain, unexplained weight loss, fatigue due to anemia, and unintended weakness. However, early-stage colon cancer may not present any noticeable signs.

Research and clinical trials for colon cancer focus on several areas including new drug therapies, immunotherapy, targeted therapy, screening methods, and prevention strategies. Specific ongoing studies may involve:

1. Investigating novel chemotherapy combinations or drugs to improve treatment efficacy while reducing side effects.

2. Developing immune checkpoint inhibitors and other forms of immuno-oncology treatments aimed at enhancing patient's own immune response against colorectal tumors.

3. Testing precision medicine approaches that target specific genetic mutations found in individual patients' cancers.

4. Evaluating advanced imaging techniques and biomarkers as tools for early detection and monitoring disease progression.

5. Studying lifestyle interventions such as diet modifications and exercise programs designed to reduce risk factors associated with developing this type of malignancy.

For detailed information about current clinical trials, one can visit websites like ClinicalTrials.gov where various phases of testing across different countries are listed.

The outlook or prognosis for rectal cancer varies depending on several factors including the stage of the disease at diagnosis, location within the rectum, patient's overall health status, response to treatment, and whether there has been any spread beyond the rectum (metastasis). Early-stage rectal cancers that have not invaded deeply into surrounding tissues generally carry better prognoses compared with advanced stages where cancer may have metastasized.

Survival rates can be used as an indicator:
- Stage I rectal cancer typically carries a 5-year survival rate around 80% - 90%
- For Stage II, this drops slightly but still remains relatively high between 60%-70%
- At Stages III & IV when it involves lymph nodes or other organs respectively, outcomes become more challenging; these stages often see lower 5-year relative survivals in ranges from about 30% down to less than 10%.

It’s important to note individual cases vary greatly so consulting healthcare professionals provides personalized information regarding specific circumstances. Treatments such as surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapies, immunotherapy etc., play crucial roles influencing recovery chances significantly. Regular follow-ups post-treatment also enhance monitoring progress effectively managing recurrence risks if applicable.

To prevent colorectal cancer, you can:

1. Get screened regularly starting at age 45 (or earlier if there is a family history or other risk factors).
2. Maintain a healthy diet rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains while limiting red meat and processed foods.
3. Exercise regularly.
4. Keep a healthy weight.
5. Avoid smoking and limit alcohol consumption.
6. Manage conditions like inflammatory bowel disease with proper treatment.

Regular screening tests such as colonoscopy help detect precancerous polyps that can be removed before they turn into cancer.

Symptoms of small intestine cancer can be vague but may include abdominal pain or discomfort, unexplained weight loss, fatigue due to anemia (iron deficiency), jaundice (yellowing of skin and eyes), nausea, vomiting, bleeding from the gastrointestinal tract which might present as black stools or blood in stool, and bowel obstruction leading to severe cramping and bloating. However, many people with early-stage small intestinal cancers do not have noticeable symptoms.

Thymoma and thymic carcinoma are both tumors that originate in the thymus gland but differ in their characteristics:

1. **Thymoma**: This is a tumor of the epithelial cells within the thymus gland, which can be benign or malignant. It often does not spread to other parts of the body even if it's cancerous.

2. **Thymic Carcinoma**: A more aggressive form of malignancy also originating from the thymus gland’s epithelial tissue, characterized by its ability to metastasize (spread) to distant sites such as lymph nodes, lungs, liver, etc., making it harder to treat compared to typical thymomas.

Research into thymoma and thymic carcinoma includes various ongoing studies aimed at improving diagnosis, treatment options, and patient outcomes. Key areas of investigation include:

1. **Immunotherapy**: Studies focusing on immune checkpoint inhibitors to enhance the body's ability to fight cancer cells.

2. **Targeted Therapies**: Research exploring specific molecular targets unique to these cancers that can be inhibited or activated to control tumor growth.

3. **Radiation Therapy Techniques**: Advances in radiation therapy techniques such as proton beam therapy and intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT).

4. **Surgical Innovations**: Improvements in surgical methods including robotic surgery and minimally invasive procedures to improve resection rates while reducing complications.

5. **Combination Treatments**: Clinical trials testing combinations of chemotherapy with other treatments like immunotherapies or targeted therapies to increase efficacy.

6. **Biomarker Identification**: Efforts to identify biomarkers predictive of response to different types of treatment which could help personalize care plans.

7. **Long-term Follow-up Programs**: Longitudinal studies tracking patients over time post-treatment to better understand recurrence patterns and long-term effects of current treatments.

For detailed information about active clinical trials, one should consult databases such as ClinicalTrials.gov or contact relevant oncology centers directly.

The prognosis of urethral cancer varies depending on factors such as tumor stage at diagnosis, location (male or female), size, grade, presence of metastasis, and patient's overall health condition. Generally, early-stage cancers have better outcomes with treatment options including surgery, radiation therapy, chemotherapy, or a combination thereof. However, due to its rarity and often late detection, many cases present in advanced stages leading to poorer survival rates compared to other genitourinary malignancies like bladder or prostate cancer. Five-year relative survival ranges from 50% to over 90%, but these figures can vary significantly between different studies and populations. Regular follow-up after initial treatment is crucial for monitoring recurrence.

Symptoms of vulvar cancer can include:

- Persistent itching or discomfort in the vulva
- Changes in skin coloration (redness, darkening)
- A lump or mass that persists 
- Bleeding not related to menstruation
- Pain during intercourse
- Unusual discharge

It's important for women experiencing these symptoms to consult with their healthcare provider for proper evaluation. Early detection improves treatment outcomes.

Treatments for vulvar cancer include surgery (such as wide local excision, lymph node dissection, or simple vulvectomy), radiation therapy, chemotherapy, and targeted therapies like immunotherapy. The specific treatment plan depends on factors such as tumor size, location, stage of disease, and patient health status. Combination approaches may be used to improve outcomes.

An aberrant subclavian artery is a congenital anomaly where one of the subclavian arteries arises from an unusual source instead of its normal origin. Typically, it originates abnormally from the opposite side's brachiocephalic trunk or the aortic arch, leading to potential vascular compression syndromes like dysphagia lusoria if it compresses adjacent structures such as the trachea or esophagus.

Abetalipoproteinemia is diagnosed through several tests including blood lipid profile which shows low levels of cholesterol and triglycerides due to reduced very-low-density lipoproteins (VLDL) and chylomicrons in the bloodstream. Additional diagnostic methods include genetic testing for mutations in the MTTP gene, fasting plasma samples analysis for absence or near-absence of beta-lipoproteins, and sometimes small bowel biopsy if malabsorption symptoms suggest tropical sprue-like syndrome. Clinical presentation with signs such as acanthocytosis, retinopathy, neurologic deficits also aids diagnosis.

Absence of tibia, also known as congenital absence or hypoplasia of the tibia, can present with several notable symptoms including:

1. Shorter leg length compared to the opposite side.
2. Deformity in the lower limb such as bowing or angular deformities if only one bone is affected.
3. Instability or weakness in the ankle and foot due to lack of proper support from the missing bone.
4. Abnormal gait pattern while walking.

These conditions often require orthopedic evaluation for management options which may include prosthetics, surgical interventions, or other supportive devices depending upon severity and associated complications.

Acatalasemia is characterized by symptoms that primarily manifest as oral lesions such as ulcerations in the mouth (fissured tongue, angular cheilitis), and there can be an increased susceptibility to infections due to catalase-positive microorganisms. In severe cases or without proper management, it may lead to necrosis of tissues like fingers under stressful conditions such as fasting or cold exposure.

The treatment for an accessory navicular bone typically depends on symptoms and severity but may include:

1. Non-surgical options:
   - Resting and avoiding activities that cause pain or discomfort.
   - Ice application to reduce inflammation.
   - Orthotic devices (shoe inserts) to support the foot structure.
   - Physical therapy exercises.

2. Surgical intervention might be considered if non-operative measures fail, including procedures like excision of the accessory bone with tendon repair or reconstruction. 

Consultation with a podiatrist or orthopedic specialist is recommended for proper diagnosis and personalized management plan.

The primary symptoms of achalasia include difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), regurgitation of food, chest pain, coughing, especially when lying down, and weight loss due to reduced intake. Patients may also experience heartburn but this is less common.

Achondrogenesis is a group of severe skeletal dysplasia conditions characterized by underdeveloped cartilage and bones, primarily affecting infants before birth or shortly after delivery. It results in extremely short stature with various bone abnormalities including very short limbs and an abnormally small chest cavity that can lead to respiratory distress. There are several subtypes distinguished mainly by genetic causes and specific clinical features.

Achondrogenesis type 1A is a severe skeletal dysplasia characterized by extreme shortening of the limbs, underdeveloped midface, and other bone abnormalities present at birth. It results from mutations in the COL2A1 gene which affects collagen synthesis necessary for proper cartilage development. This condition is usually fatal early in life due to respiratory problems or heart defects.

The primary symptoms of achondroplasia include:
- Short stature with disproportionately short arms and legs
- A large head relative to body size 
- Prominent forehead (frontal bossing)
- Narrow nasal bridge
- Increased curvature of the lower back (lordosis) and sometimes swayback (kyphosis)
- Limited range of motion at elbows
- Dental issues due to small maxilla (upper jaw)

These physical characteristics result from abnormal cartilage formation during bone growth in this genetic disorder.

Achondroplasia is characterized by:
- Short stature with disproportionately short arms and legs
- A large head relative to body size 
- Prominent forehead

Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) typically presents as:
- Recurrent or persistent infections 
- Failure to thrive
- Pneumonias, sinusitis, oral thrush in infants
- Diarrhea and skin abscesses

These conditions have distinct symptom profiles - achondroplasia affects bone growth while SCID impacts immune function severely. They would present very differently clinically.

Acquired Pure Red Cell Aplasia (PRCA) is a rare condition characterized by anemia resulting from the bone marrow's failure to produce erythroblasts (red blood cell precursors), while other types of blood cells like leukocytes and thrombocytes remain unaffected in their production. This leads to a significant decrease or absence of developing red blood cells, causing severe anemia. It can be caused by various factors including drugs, infections, autoimmune diseases, thymomas, and parvovirus B19 infection among others. Treatment depends on identifying and addressing the underlying cause.

Acrodermatitis enteropathica is a rare genetic disorder characterized by zinc deficiency, leading to skin lesions typically around the nails, hair loss, diarrhea, and immune system problems. It results from mutations in the SLC39A4 gene which encodes for a protein involved in zinc absorption. Treatment involves lifelong zinc supplementation.

Acrokeratoelastoidosis of Costa is characterized by asymptomatic small, yellow to skin-colored papules or nodules typically found in the dorsum (top) of fingers and hands. These lesions have a firm consistency due to abnormal elastic tissue within them. They do not usually cause pain or itching unless irritated.

Acromesomelic dysplasia refers to a group of rare genetic disorders characterized by severe shortening of the long bones in the hands, feet, forearms, and lower legs. This condition affects bone growth primarily in the middle segments of fingers and toes as well as distal parts like finger tips. There are several subtypes including types Maroteaux type I, Maroteaux Type II, and Bohnsack-Champion-Mitchell syndrome, each with slightly different clinical presentations but all sharing similar skeletal abnormalities.

Acro-renal-mandibular Syndrome (ARM) is characterized by specific physical features including:

1. Abnormalities in fingers/toes such as brachydactyly (shortening), syndactyly (fusion between digits).
2. Renal anomalies like hypoplastic kidneys or renal agenesis (absence of one or both kidneys).
3. Mandibular abnormalities which can include micrognathia (small jaw).

Other associated signs may involve eye defects, hearing loss, heart issues, and genital malformations. Symptoms vary among affected individuals due to variable expression within this genetic disorder.

Acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis, also known as Sweet's syndrome, is a skin condition characterized by sudden onset of fever, presence of painful or tender skin lesions, and elevated levels of white blood cells called neutrophils in both the bloodstream and affected areas of the skin. It can be associated with underlying systemic conditions such as infections, malignancies, or autoimmune diseases.

5. **Cytogenetic Analysis & Fluorescence In Situ Hybridization (FISH):** These genetic analyses help identify chromosomal abnormalities associated with certain subtypes of leukemia.

6. **Immunophenotyping Tests:** Determine whether lymphoid or myeloid lineage is affected through surface markers expressed on cells.

Doctors use staging systems to describe the extent of cancer progression in bones, most commonly using either the TNM system (Tumor size, Node involvement, Metastasis) or numerical staging from Stage I to IV.

1. **TNM System**:
   - T describes the primary tumor's size and location.
     - TX means the main tumor cannot be assessed.
     - T0 indicates no evidence of a primary tumor.
     - T1-T4 indicate increasing sizes/locations of tumors.
   - N refers to lymph nodes near the affected area.
     - NX signifies nearby regional lymph node evaluation is not done.
     - N0 shows there’s no metastatic disease in these nodes.
     - N1-N3 denote progressively higher levels of nodal involvement.
   - M represents distant metastases.
     - MX stands for unknown status regarding distant sites.
     - M0 states there are no known secondary cancers elsewhere.
     - M1 denotes presence of one or multiple secondary cancers at different body parts.

2. **Numerical Staging (I-IV)**:
   - **Stage 1**: The tumor is localized within the bone with low-grade cells (less aggressive).
   - **Stage 2**: Similar to stage 1 but involves high-grade cells (more aggressive).
   - **Stages 3 & 4**: These involve larger tumors, possibly affecting adjacent tissues; may also include cases where cancerous cells have spread beyond the initial site into surrounding tissue or organs

2. **Immunotherapy**: Trials involving immune checkpoint inhibitors which help boost the body’s own ability to fight off tumors by enhancing T-cell activity.

3. **Photodynamic Therapy (PDT)**: This involves using light-activated medications to destroy tumor cells while minimizing damage to healthy tissue.

4. **Voice Rehabilitation Techniques**: Research into better methods for restoring speech after treatment-induced vocal impairment through surgical techniques such as laryngotracheal separation surgery combined with esophageal speech training, use of electronic devices, or tracheoesophageal puncture prostheses.

5. **Radiation Therapy Advances**: Improvements in radiation therapy delivery including intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT), proton beam therapy, and stereotactic ablative radiotherapy aimed at reducing side effects while improving efficacy.

6. **Combination Treatments**: Clinical studies exploring combinations of chemotherapy, targeted therapies, immunotherapies, and/or radiation to enhance effectiveness over single-agent approaches.

7. **Early Detection Methods**: Development of biomarkers and imaging technologies capable of detecting early-stage disease more effectively than current standard practices.

These advancements collectively seek not only improved survival rates but also enhanced quality of life post-treatment particularly concerning functional outcomes related to swallowing and speaking

Treatment for cancers of the mouth, throat (including areas near the tonsils) typically depends on several factors including the stage of the tumor, its location, size, whether it has spread to other parts of the body, as well as patient's overall health.

Common treatments include:

1. **Surgery**: To remove tumors directly from the affected tissues such as removing part of the tongue, jawbone, lymph nodes, etc., depending upon where the cancer is located.
   
2. **Radiation Therapy**: Often used alone if the tumor is small enough but can also complement surgical removals post-surgically to kill any remaining microscopic cells. It uses high-energy rays to shrink or eliminate tumors.

3. **Chemotherapy**: Can either be administered systemically through pills or intravenous drugs targeting rapidly dividing cells throughout the entire body, often combined with radiation therapy especially when dealing with more advanced stages of head and neck cancers.

4. **Targeted Drug Therapies** & Immunotherapies: These newer approaches target specific molecules involved in carcinogenesis without affecting normal healthy tissue much as possible.

The severity at which these conditions require different treatment modalities usually hinges on:
- The exact site within the oral cavity/throat,
- Size and aggressiveness of the primary lesion,
- Presence/absence of metastasis elsewhere in the body via imaging studies and biopsies.

The staging of oral cavity and oropharyngeal cancers typically follows the TNM system (Tumor, Node, Metastasis):

1. **Stage I**: The tumor is small (<2 cm) and has not spread to lymph nodes or distant sites.

2. **Stage II**: The primary tumor measures between 2-4 cm and there's no evidence it has spread beyond this region; regional lymph nodes may be involved but without metastases elsewhere.

3. **Stages III & IV**:
   - Stage III can involve larger tumors (>4cm), involvement of nearby structures such as bone, teeth, or muscles with possible nodal involvement.
   - Stage IV includes very large tumors that have invaded surrounding tissues extensively, significant node involvement including those outside the neck, or presence of distant metastatic disease.

Doctors use imaging studies (like CT scans, MRIs), physical exams, biopsies, and sometimes PET scans to determine these factors for accurate staging which guides treatment planning from least invasive options at earlier stages to more aggressive treatments needed later on.

It sounds like you might be referring to gastric cancer, which can affect the stomach (often called "belly gland" colloquially). Gastric cancer starts when cells in the lining of the stomach begin to grow abnormally and uncontrollably.

- In more advanced stages, it could spread beyond the stomach into other organs or lymph nodes, leading to severe complications including obstruction of the digestive tract, perforation of the stomach wall causing infection, or metastasis affecting distant parts of the body like liver, lungs, bones, etc., potentially becoming life-threatening. 

Treatment options include surgery, chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted drug treatments, immunotherapy depending upon stage at diagnosis. Early detection improves outcomes significantly.

Doctors use staging systems to describe how advanced stomach (gastric) cancer is, typically using either the TNM system or an overall stage grouping:

1. **TNM System**:
   - Tumor size (T): Describes the primary tumor's size and whether it has invaded nearby tissues.
     - TX: Primary tumor cannot be assessed.
     - T0: No evidence of a primary tumor.
     - T1-T4: Increasing sizes and invasions into deeper layers of tissue.

   - Lymph Nodes involvement (N):
     - NX: Regional lymph nodes cannot be evaluated.
     - N0: No regional lymph node metastasis.
     - N1-N3: Indicates increasing levels of lymph node involvement.

   - Metastases (M):
     - MX: Distant metastasis cannot be assessed.
     - M0: No distant metastasis.
     - M1: Presence of distant metastasis.

2. **Overall Stage Grouping**:
   - Stage I: Cancer limited to the innermost lining of the stomach wall with no lymph node involvement.
   - Stage II: Involves more extensive invasion within the stomach wall but still without spreading beyond the abdomen; may involve some local lymph nodes.
   - Stage III: More invasive disease involving adjacent organs or major blood vessels, often including significant lymph node involvement.
   - Stage IV: The most severe form where there’s widespread dissemination through other parts of the body such as liver, lungs, bones

Doctors diagnose unusual hormone-producing tumors (also known as neuroendocrine tumors) through several steps:

4. **Endoscopy/Colonoscopy**: If gastrointestinal issues are suspected, an endoscope may be used to directly view inside the digestive tract looking for lesions.

Multiple myeloma, which is a type of blood and bone marrow cancer involving abnormal plasma cells, progresses through several stages as it worsens:

1. **Smoldering Myeloma (Asymptomatic):** This stage involves an increased number of malignant plasma cells in the bone marrow but no symptoms such as bone pain, kidney problems, low red blood counts, high calcium levels, etc.

2. **Active Multiple Myeloma:** Once patients start experiencing related health issues due to their condition, they move into active multiple myeloma. It can be further divided into:
   - Stage I: Patients have fewer than 30% involvement by clonal plasma cells in the bone marrow; normal beta-2 microglobulin level (<3.5 mg/L); and/or light chain ratio less than 18. 
   - Stage II: More advanced with intermediate disease burden between Stages I & III criteria.
   - Stage III: The most severe form where there's significant tumor load, higher serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels, greater than 60% bone marrow plasmacytosis, more extensive lytic lesions, elevated beta-2-microglobulin (>5.5 mg/L), and/or very high M-protein concentration.

Doctors determine the staging using various tests including physical exams, imaging studies (like X-rays, MRI, CT scans), lab work assessing protein levels in the blood and urine, and measuring specific markers

- Secondary (or metastatic) malignancies occur when cancerous cells spread to the liver from other organs such as colon, lung, breast, etc., forming new tumor masses there.

The key difference lies in their origin; while both types involve abnormal growths in the liver tissue, only those classified under "primary" actually originate directly from hepatic cells.    - Tumor size (T)
     - TX indicates that tumor size cannot be assessed.
     - T0 means no evidence of primary tumor.
     - T1-T4 describes increasing sizes or numbers of tumors within the liver.
   - Lymph Node involvement (N):
     - NX signifies lymph node status can't be evaluated; N0 shows no spread to nearby nodes while N1 confirms it has spread.
   - Metastasis (M): 
     - MX denotes metastatic information unavailable; M0 states there's been no distant spreading whereas M1 affirms such dissemination.

2. **American Joint Committee on Cancer (AJCC) Staging** builds upon TNM by assigning numerical values from Stage I through IV reflecting severity:
    - **Stage I:** Single tumor without vascular invasion.
    - **Stage II:** Multiple nodules confined within the same lobe with no major vessel infiltration.
    - **Stage IIIA & B:** Presence of one or more large (>5 cm), multiple lesions across both lobes, or significant blood vessel invasion but still localized to the liver.
    - **Stage IVA:** Spread beyond the confines of the peritoneal cavity.
    - **Stage IVB:** Distant organ metastases outside the abdomen like lungs, bones etc., indicating advanced disease.

The exact stage helps guide treatment options and prognosis estimation

The condition you're referring to is called Langerhans cell histiocytosis (LCH). It involves an abnormal accumulation of Langerhans cells, which are specialized dendritic cells usually found within tissues like skin, lymphoid tissue, liver, spleen, lungs, and bones. This buildup can lead to various symptoms including rashes, bone lesions, and other systemic effects.

While not strictly classified as a type of cancer because these accumulations do not originate from transformed cells but rather overactive normal ones, LCH shares some characteristics with cancers due to its potential for spread throughout different organs and systems. However, unlike typical malignancies, there's no uncontrolled growth of mutated cells; instead, it results from excessive proliferation and/or survival of normally functioning immune cells leading to pathological consequences. Treatment approaches may include chemotherapy-like drugs used also against true neoplastic diseases given their effectiveness at suppressing such proliferative conditions.

Langerhans Cell Histiocytosis (LCH) is characterized by varying presentations rather than distinct "stages." However, its progression can be described in terms of affected organs/systems:

2. **Multifocal/Multi-system disease**:
   - Two-bone lesions not contiguous with each other 
   - More than two bones involved
   - Any single extracranial lesion plus any number of non-contiguous bone lesions
   - Multiple systems involvement

Progression varies widely depending on which parts of the body are affected. Some patients may have self-limiting disease that resolves spontaneously without treatment, while others might experience progressive multi-organ dysfunction requiring aggressive therapy. The prognosis depends largely on the extent of disease at diagnosis, age of patient, and specific sites involved; for instance, central nervous system involvement often indicates more severe cases. Treatment strategies range from observation alone to chemotherapy, immunotherapy, radiation therapy, and sometimes surgery. Regular follow-up is essential due to potential late effects even after successful initial management.

A doctor determines whether a rapidly growing skin lesion might be an aggressive form of skin cancer by first conducting a thorough clinical examination to assess its appearance (size, shape, color), location, texture, and any associated symptoms like pain or bleeding.

To confirm diagnosis:
1. **Biopsy**: The most definitive method involves taking a sample of tissue for microscopic analysis in a pathology lab. This could involve excisional biopsy where the entire suspicious area is removed; punch biopsy where a small cylindrical tool removes a section of the growth; or shave biopsy where only part of the surface layer is taken off with a scalpel.

2. **Imaging Studies**: In some cases, imaging such as ultrasound, CT scan, MRI, or PET scans may help evaluate deeper tissues involvement or lymph node spread which isn't visible during physical exam alone.

3. **Histopathological Examination**: After obtaining samples via one of these methods, pathologists examine cells under microscope looking specifically at cell morphology indicative of malignancy versus normal/benign changes. For instance, melanoma shows irregularly shaped nuclei, pleomorphism (variety in size/shape) among others compared to keratosis that has more uniform features.

4. **Differential Diagnosis**: To differentiate between malignant lesions and harmless ones like seborrheic keratoses, warts, cysts etc., doctors consider patient history including age, sun exposure habits along with visual characteristics unique to each condition mentioned above alongside histology results post-biopsy

2. Wear protective clothing such as long sleeves, pants, hats, and sunglasses.
3. Seek shade between peak hours of UV exposure (usually midday).
4. Avoid tanning beds and excessive sunlight.
5. Examine your skin regularly for changes in moles or new growths.

These practices help reduce risk factors associated with harmful ultraviolet radiation that leads to premature aging and potential malignancies.

Multiple Myeloma is typically classified into three main clinical stages using the International Staging System (ISS), which primarily relies on levels of beta-2 microglobulin and serum albumin:

1. **Stage I**: This stage indicates lower disease burden with relatively normal life expectancy. It's characterized by:
   - Beta-2 Microglobulin <3.5 mg/L,
   - Serum Albumin ≥ 3.5 g/dL.

2. **Stage II**: Indicates an intermediate level of disease activity between Stage I and III. Patients may have features that fall outside both categories or show slightly elevated markers but not to the extent seen in advanced cases.
   
3. **Stage III**: Represents more aggressive disease with higher risk factors for complications and shorter survival without treatment. Markers include:
    - Beta-2 Microglobulin >5.5 mg/L OR 
    - Any value if Serum Albumin <3.0 g/dL AND Beta-2 Microglobulin >3.5 mg/L

Additionally, some clinicians use other staging systems like Durie-Salmon criteria, though it has largely been replaced by ISS due to its simplicity and better correlation with patient outcomes. These classifications help guide therapeutic decisions and predict prognosis.

SCLC typically grows rapidly and metastasizes early compared to non-small cell lung cancers, often spreading to lymph nodes and distant organs like bones, brain, liver, and adrenal glands.

Aggressive chest cancers, primarily lung cancer but also potentially involving other thoracic structures like mediastinal tumors, can be treated with various methods depending on factors such as tumor stage, location, patient health status, and specific genetic characteristics of the tumor.

1. **Surgery**: For early-stage non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), surgical resection is often recommended if the patient's overall condition allows it. This may include lobectomy (removal of one lobe) or pneumonectomy (complete removal of an affected lung).

2. **Chemotherapy**: Often combined with radiation therapy in advanced stages to reduce tumor size before surgery ("neoadjuvant") or after surgery ("adjuvant"). It’s commonly administered systemically through intravenous infusion targeting rapidly dividing cells throughout the body.

3. **Radiation Therapy**: Can be delivered externally using high-energy beams aimed at the tumor site from outside the body. In some cases, internal radiation ('brachytherapy') might involve placing radioactive material directly into or near the tumor.

4. **Targeted Therapies & Immunotherapies**: These newer forms target specific molecular pathways involved in cancer growth or enhance immune response against cancerous tissue respectively. They're particularly useful when certain biomarkers are present within the tumor.

5. **Palliative Care**: Focuses more broadly on symptom management rather than curative intent, especially beneficial during later disease states where quality-of-life improvements become paramount over extending life expectancy.

An aggressive type of brain tumor similar to malignant astrocytomas includes Glioblastoma Multiforme (GBM), which is considered one of the most severe forms of astrocytic tumors. GBMs are classified as Grade IV under the World Health Organization's grading system for central nervous system tumors.

While "brain cancer" can refer broadly to any malignancy within or affecting the brain tissue, including various types like gliomas, meningiomas, lymphomas, etc., a malignant astrocytoma specifically refers to cancers that originate in star-shaped glial cells known as astrocytes found throughout the brain. 

Glioblastoma multiforme differs by being characterized by rapid growth, high cellularity with significant necrosis and associated edema, along with areas of hemorrhage and cystic changes. It also has genetic alterations such as mutations in IDH1/2 genes less commonly seen compared to lower-grade gliomas but more frequent than normal brain tissues. Additionally, GBM often shows increased expression of epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) amplification and promoter methylation of MGMT gene. These features make GBM particularly invasive and difficult to treat effectively due to its diffuse nature across brain parenchyma.

reference_answers: Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose adult ALL. The following tests and procedures may be used: - Physical exam and history : An exam of the body to check general signs of health, including checking for signs of disease, such as infection or anything else that seems unusual. A history of the patient's health habits and past illnesses and treatments will also be taken. - Complete blood count (CBC) with differential : A procedure in which a sample of blood is drawn and checked for the following: - The number of red blood cells and platelets. - The number and type of white blood cells. - The amount of hemoglobin (the protein that carries oxygen) in the red blood cells. - The portion of the blood sample made up of red blood cells. - Blood chemistry studies : A procedure in which a blood sample is checked to measure the amounts of certain substances released into the blood by organs and tissues in the body. An unusual (higher or lower than normal) amount of a substance can be a sign of disease. - Peripheral blood smear : A procedure in which a sample of blood is checked for blast cells, the number and kinds of white blood cells, the number of platelets, and changes in the shape of blood cells. - Bone marrow aspiration and biopsy : The removal of bone marrow, blood, and a small piece of bone by inserting a hollow needle into the hipbone or breastbone. A pathologist views the bone marrow, blood, and bone under a microscope to look for abnormal cells. The following tests may be done on the samples of blood or bone marrow tissue that are removed: - Cytogenetic analysis: A laboratory test in which the cells in a sample of blood or bone marrow are looked at under a microscope to find out if there are certain changes in the chromosomes of lymphocytes. For example, in Philadelphia chromosome positive ALL, part of one chromosome switches places with part of another chromosome. This is called the Philadelphia chromosome. - Immunophenotyping : A process used to identify cells, based on the types of antigens or markers on the surface of the cell. This process is used to diagnose the subtype of ALL by comparing the cancer cells to normal cells of the immune system. For example, a cytochemistry study may test the cells in a sample of tissue using chemicals (dyes) to look for certain changes in the sample. A chemical may cause a color change in one type of leukemia cell but not in another type of leukemia cell.

Key Points - Adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes abnormal myeloblasts (a type of white blood cell), red blood cells, or platelets. - Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. - There are different subtypes of AML. - Smoking, previous chemotherapy treatment, and exposure to radiation may affect the risk of adult AML. - Signs and symptoms of adult AML include fever, feeling tired, and easy bruising or bleeding. - Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose adult AML. - Certain factors affect prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options. Adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a type of cancer in which the bone marrow makes abnormal myeloblasts (a type of white blood cell), red blood cells, or platelets. Adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) is a cancer of the blood and bone marrow. This type of cancer usually gets worse quickly if it is not treated. It is the most common type of acute leukemia in adults. AML is also called acute myelogenous leukemia, acute myeloblastic leukemia, acute granulocytic leukemia, and acute nonlymphocytic leukemia. Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Normally, the bone marrow makes blood stem cells (immature cells) that become mature blood cells over time. A blood stem cell may become a myeloid stem cell or a lymphoid stem cell. A lymphoid stem cell becomes a white blood cell. A myeloid stem cell becomes one of three types of mature blood cells: - Red blood cells that carry oxygen and other substances to all tissues of the body. - White blood cells that fight infection and disease. - Platelets that form blood clots to stop bleeding. In AML, the myeloid stem cells usually become a type of immature white blood cell called myeloblasts (or myeloid blasts). The myeloblasts in AML are abnormal and do not become healthy white blood cells. Sometimes in AML, too many stem cells become abnormal red blood cells or platelets. These abnormal white blood cells, red blood cells, or platelets are also called leukemia cells or blasts. Leukemia cells can build up in the bone marrow and blood so there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. When this happens, infection, anemia, or easy bleeding may occur. The leukemia cells can spread outside the blood to other parts of the body, including the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord), skin, and gums. This summary is about adult AML. See the following PDQ summaries for information about other types of leukemia: - Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia/Other Myeloid Malignancies Treatment - Chronic Myelogenous Leukemia Treatment - Adult Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment - Childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment - Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia Treatment - Hairy Cell Leukemia Treatment There are different subtypes of AML. Most AML subtypes are based on how mature (developed) the cancer cells are at the time of diagnosis and how different they are from normal cells. Acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL) is a subtype of AML that occurs when parts of two genes stick together. APL usually occurs in middle-aged adults. Signs of APL may include both bleeding and forming blood clots.

Key Points - Once adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. - There is no standard staging system for adult AML. Once adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML) has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread to other parts of the body. The extent or spread of cancer is usually described as stages. In adult acute myeloid leukemia (AML), the subtype of AML and whether the leukemia has spread outside the blood and bone marrow are used instead of the stage to plan treatment. The following tests and procedures may be used to determine if the leukemia has spread: - Lumbar puncture : A procedure used to collect a sample of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) from the spinal column. This is done by placing a needle between two bones in the spine and into the CSF around the spinal cord and removing a sample of the fluid. The sample of CSF is checked under a microscope for signs that leukemia cells have spread to the brain and spinal cord. This procedure is also called an LP or spinal tap. - CT scan (CAT scan): A procedure that makes a series of detailed pictures of the abdomen, taken from different angles. The pictures are made by a computer linked to an x-ray machine. A dye may be injected into a vein or swallowed to help the organs or tissues show up more clearly. This procedure is also called computed tomography, computerized tomography, or computerized axial tomography. There is no standard staging system for adult AML. The disease is described as untreated, in remission, or recurrent. Untreated adult AML In untreated adult AML, the disease is newly diagnosed. It has not been treated except to relieve signs and symptoms such as fever, bleeding, or pain, and the following are true: - The complete blood count is abnormal. - At least 20% of the cells in the bone marrow are blasts (leukemia cells). - There are signs or symptoms of leukemia. Adult AML in remission In adult AML in remission, the disease has been treated and the following are true: - The complete blood count is normal. - Less than 5% of the cells in the bone marrow are blasts (leukemia cells). - There are no signs or symptoms of leukemia in the brain and spinal cord or elsewhere in the body. Recurrent Adult AML Recurrent AML is cancer that has recurred (come back) after it has been treated. The AML may come back in the blood or bone marrow.

Signs and symptoms of chronic lymphocytic leukemia include swollen lymph nodes and tiredness. Usually CLL does not cause any signs or symptoms and is found during a routine blood test. Signs and symptoms may be caused by CLL or by other conditions. Check with your doctor if you have any of the following: - Painless swelling of the lymph nodes in the neck, underarm, stomach, or groin. - Feeling very tired. - Pain or fullness below the ribs. - Fever and infection. - Weight loss for no known reason.

Key Points - Chronic myelogenous leukemia is a disease in which the bone marrow makes too many white blood cells. - Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. - Signs and symptoms of chronic myelogenous leukemia include fever, night sweats, and tiredness. - Most people with CML have a gene mutation (change) called the Philadelphia chromosome. - Tests that examine the blood and bone marrow are used to detect (find) and diagnose chronic myelogenous leukemia. - Certain factors affect prognosis (chance of recovery) and treatment options. Chronic myelogenous leukemia is a disease in which the bone marrow makes too many white blood cells. Chronic myelogenous leukemia (also called CML or chronic granulocytic leukemia) is a slowly progressing blood and bone marrow disease that usually occurs during or after middle age, and rarely occurs in children. Leukemia may affect red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Normally, the bone marrow makes blood stem cells (immature cells) that become mature blood cells over time. A blood stem cell may become a myeloid stem cell or a lymphoid stem cell. A lymphoid stem cell becomes a white blood cell. A myeloid stem cell becomes one of three types of mature blood cells: - Red blood cells that carry oxygen and other substances to all tissues of the body. - Platelets that form blood clots to stop bleeding. - Granulocytes (white blood cells) that fight infection and disease. In CML, too many blood stem cells become a type of white blood cell called granulocytes. These granulocytes are abnormal and do not become healthy white blood cells. They are also called leukemia cells. The leukemia cells can build up in the blood and bone marrow so there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. When this happens, infection, anemia, or easy bleeding may occur. This summary is about chronic myelogenous leukemia. See the following PDQ summaries for more information about leukemia: - Adult Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment - Childhood Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia Treatment - Adult Acute Myeloid Leukemia Treatment - Childhood Acute Myeloid Leukemia/Other Myeloid Malignancies Treatment - Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia Treatment - Hairy Cell Leukemia Treatment

Key Points - After chronic myelogenous leukemia has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread. - Chronic myelogenous leukemia has 3 phases. - Chronic phase - Accelerated phase - Blastic phase After chronic myelogenous leukemia has been diagnosed, tests are done to find out if the cancer has spread. Staging is the process used to find out how far the cancer has spread. There is no standard staging system for chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML). Instead, the disease is classified by phase: chronic phase, accelerated phase, or blastic phase. It is important to know the phase in order to plan treatment. The information from tests and procedures done to detect (find) and diagnose chronic myelogenous leukemia is also used to plan treatment. Chronic myelogenous leukemia has 3 phases. As the amount of blast cells increases in the blood and bone marrow, there is less room for healthy white blood cells, red blood cells, and platelets. This may result in infections, anemia, and easy bleeding, as well as bone pain and pain or a feeling of fullness below the ribs on the left side. The number of blast cells in the blood and bone marrow and the severity of signs or symptoms determine the phase of the disease. Chronic phase In chronic phase CML, fewer than 10% of the cells in the blood and bone marrow are blast cells. Accelerated phase In accelerated phase CML, 10% to 19% of the cells in the blood and bone marrow are blast cells. Blastic phase In blastic phase CML, 20% or more of the cells in the blood or bone marrow are blast cells. When tiredness, fever, and an enlarged spleen occur during the blastic phase, it is called blast crisis.

Signs and symptoms of hairy cell leukemia include infections, tiredness, and pain below the ribs. These and other signs and symptoms may be caused by hairy cell leukemia or by other conditions. Check with your doctor if you have any of the following: - Weakness or feeling tired. - Fever or frequent infections. - Easy bruising or bleeding. - Shortness of breath. - Weight loss for no known reason. - Pain or a feeling of fullness below the ribs. - Painless lumps in the neck, underarm, stomach, or groin.

Key Points - There are different types of treatment for patients with hairy cell leukemia. - Five types of standard treatment are used: - Watchful waiting - Chemotherapy - Biologic therapy - Surgery - Targeted therapy - New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials. - Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. - Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment. - Follow-up tests may be needed. There are different types of treatment for patients with hairy cell leukemia. Different types of treatment are available for patients with hairy cell leukemia. Some treatments are standard (the currently used treatment), and some are being tested in clinical trials. A treatment clinical trial is a research study meant to help improve current treatments or obtain information on new treatments for patients with cancer. When clinical trials show that a new treatment is better than the standard treatment, the new treatment may become the standard treatment. Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. Some clinical trials are open only to patients who have not started treatment. Five types of standard treatment are used: Watchful waiting Watchful waiting is closely monitoring a patient's condition, without giving any treatment until signs or symptoms appear or change. Chemotherapy Chemotherapy is a cancer treatment that uses drugs to stop the growth of cancer cells, either by killing the cells or by stopping them from dividing. When chemotherapy is taken by mouth or injected into a vein or muscle, the drugs enter the bloodstream and can reach cancer cells throughout the body (systemic chemotherapy). When chemotherapy is placed directly into the cerebrospinal fluid, an organ, or a body cavity such as the abdomen, the drugs mainly affect cancer cells in those areas (regional chemotherapy). The way the chemotherapy is given depends on the type and stage of the cancer being treated. Cladribine and pentostatin are anticancer drugs commonly used to treat hairy cell leukemia. These drugs may increase the risk of other types of cancer, especially Hodgkin lymphoma and non-Hodgkin lymphoma. Long-term follow up for second cancers is very important. Biologic therapy Biologic therapy is a cancer treatment that uses the patients immune system to fight cancer. Substances made by the body or made in a laboratory are used to boost, direct, or restore the bodys natural defenses against cancer. This type of cancer treatment is also called biotherapy or immunotherapy. Interferon alfa is a biologic agent commonly used to treat hairy cell leukemia. See Drugs Approved for Hairy Cell Leukemia for more information. Surgery Splenectomy is a surgical procedure to remove the spleen. Targeted therapy Targeted therapy is a treatment that uses drugs or other substances to identify and attack specific cancer cells without harming normal cells. Monoclonal antibody therapy is a type of targeted therapy used to treat hairy cell leukemia. Monoclonal antibody therapy uses antibodies made in the laboratory from a single type of immune system cell. These antibodies can identify substances on cancer cells or normal substances that may help cancer cells grow. The antibodies attach to the substances and kill the cancer cells, block their growth, or keep them from spreading. Monoclonal antibodies are given by infusion. They may be used alone or to carry drugs, toxins, or radioactive material directly to cancer cells. A monoclonal antibody called rituximab may be used for certain patients with hairy cell leukemia. Other types of targeted therapies are being studied. New types of treatment are being tested in clinical trials. Information about clinical trials is available from the NCI website. Patients may want to think about taking part in a clinical trial. For some patients, taking part in a clinical trial may be the best treatment choice. Many of today's standard treatments for cancer are based on earlier clinical trials. Patients who take part in a clinical trial may receive the standard treatment or be among the first to receive a new treatment. Patients who take part in clinical trials also help improve the way cancer will be treated in the future. Even when clinical trials do not lead to effective new treatments, they often answer important questions and help move research forward. Patients can enter clinical trials before, during, or after starting their cancer treatment. Some clinical trials only include patients who have not yet received treatment. Other trials test treatments for patients whose cancer has not gotten better. Signs and symptoms of childhood AML, childhood CML, JMML, or MDS include fever, feeling tired, and easy bleeding or bruising. These and other signs and symptoms may be caused by childhood AML, childhood CML, JMML, or MDS or by other conditions. Check with a doctor if your child has any of the following: - Fever with or without an infection. - Night sweats. - Shortness of breath. - Weakness or feeling tired. - Easy bruising or bleeding. - Petechiae (flat, pinpoint spots under the skin caused by bleeding). - Pain in the bones or joints. - Pain or feeling of fullness below the ribs. - Painless lumps in the neck, underarm, stomach, groin, or other parts of the body. In childhood AML, these lumps, called leukemia cutis, may be blue or purple. - Painless lumps that are sometimes around the eyes. These lumps, called chloromas, are sometimes seen in childhood AML and may be blue-green. - An eczema -like skin rash. The signs and symptoms of TMD may include the following: - Swelling all over the body. - Shortness of breath. - Trouble breathing. - Weakness or feeling tired. - Pain below the ribs.
